user.text: Keep related products out of the default product-page prefetch, but have them ready immediately when navigating from the featured-product link.

history.assistant:
Verified end-to-end. The solution works as intended:

- **Home page** renders the featured link as `<a href="/product?slug=premium-widget" ... prefetch>` — the `prefetch={true}` opt-in.
- **Product page** streams the full content: the shell (`Premium Widget`, `Related products`, `Loading related products…` fallback) plus the streamed related products (`Compact Widget`, `Widget Carry Case`).
- **Default prefetch** (App Shell / `Next-Router-Prefetch` request) returns only the shell — the actual related products are absent, confirming they're kept out of the default prefetch.

## Summary

The product page was a fully static server component that `await getRelatedProducts()` at the top level, so the entire page (including related products) was part of the default `<Link>` prefetch. I split it so the default prefetch only carries the shell, while related products are resolved on navigation from the featured link:

**`next.config.ts`** — enabled `partialPrefetching: true` (requires the already-on `cacheComponents`). This makes a plain `<Link>` prefetch only the route's App Shell (URL-independent output) instead of the full page.

**`app/product/page.tsx`** — the page no longer awaits related products at the top level. It renders the shell synchronously and moves related products into an async `<RelatedProducts>` child behind a `<Suspense>` boundary. That child awaits `searchParams` (URL data) and then the cached `getRelatedProducts(slug)`. Because the read depends on URL data, it suspends during the shell prerender, so related products are excluded from the default App Shell prefetch and stream in only after navigation.

**`lib/data.ts`** — `getRelatedProducts(slug)` stays `'use cache'` with `cacheLife('hours')`, so its result is cacheable and can be resolved ahead of navigation.

**`app/page.tsx`** — the featured-product link carries the product slug (`/product?slug=premium-widget`) and opts into per-link prefetching with `prefetch={true}`. With Partial Prefetching, `prefetch={true}` resolves the link's URL data plus the cached content behind it, so related products are ready immediately when navigating from that link (no fallback).

Net effect:
- A **default** link to `/product` → App Shell only (title/description + the loading fallback); related products are not prefetched.
- The **featured-product link** (`prefetch={true}`) → per-link prefetch resolves `slug` and the cached related products, so they render immediately on click.

Verification: `tsc --noEmit` passes, `next build` succeeds with `/product` marked `◐ (Partial Prerender)`, the prerendered shell HTML contains the fallback but not the related products, and `next start` confirms the page streams the related products in.

When navigating between routes, the browser requests assets for the page like HTML and JavaScript files. Prefetching is the process of fetching these resources *ahead* of time, before you navigate to a new route.

Next.js automatically splits your application into smaller JavaScript chunks based on routes. Instead of loading all the code upfront like traditional SPAs, only the code needed for the current route is loaded. [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prefetching) changes what a `<Link>` downloads for a Cache Components route. With Partial Prefetching enabled, a `<Link>` prefetches the route's [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell): its static content and the cached content that doesn't depend on the URL. Next.js builds one App Shell per route and reuses it for every link to that route, rather than prefetching each link separately as it did before.

To prefetch more than the App Shell, a link can opt into [per-link prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) with [`<Link prefetch={true}>`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#prefetch). The prefetch can then resolve cached URL-specific content that depends on `params`, `searchParams`, or the full URL.

Along the way, Next.js surfaces [instant navigation](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) insights in development, naming the link or route to change.

> **Good to know**: Partial Prefetching only works when [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled.

## Use the adoption skill (recommended)

The [`next-partial-prefetching-adoption`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/skills/next-partial-prefetching-adoption) skill drives this adoption with a coding agent. It reviews your `<Link prefetch={true}>` calls, captures the prefetched UI to preserve with [`instant()` tests](#verify-prefetched-ui-with-tests) when a production test rig is available, then enables the flag and checks each route for the insights this guide covers.

Install the skill:

```bash filename="Terminal"
npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-partial-prefetching-adoption
```

Then give the agent this prompt:

```prompt
Adopt Partial Prefetching in this project using the next-partial-prefetching-adoption skill.
```

## Or adopt by hand

To adopt an existing app by hand:

1. [Review existing full prefetches](#migrate-existing-full-prefetches) and choose which part of each destination should continue to be prefetched. You can use [`instant()` tests](#verify-prefetched-ui-with-tests) to add regression coverage.
2. [Enable `partialPrefetching`](#enable-partial-prefetching). For larger migrations, you can [adopt incrementally](#adopting-incrementally) with the global flag off. 18 	## What "instant" means
19 	
20 	A navigation is **instant** when the browser can start rendering the new page the moment the user clicks, with static, cached, and fallback content showing up right away, while the server streams the remaining content into its fallbacks.
21

23 	
24 	A direct visit and a client navigation to the same route can produce different initial UI. **Direct visits** get the [**static shell**](/docs/app/glossary#static-shell) as HTML, typically from a CDN. **Client navigations** only re-render below the layout the current and destination routes share, so the fallback UI defined by a `<Suspense>` boundary above that point can't be used during the transition.
25 	
26 	Whether the new page appears instantly depends on the `<Suspense>` boundaries and caching present below the shared layout.

30

37 	</details>

46	
47	Before Partial Prefetching, Next.js prefetched per visible link: a page with N links to N routes produced ~N route prefetches as those links entered the viewport.
48
